title: Put a bench plane back together after honing: iron onto both adjusters, lever cap hooked and cam locked
instruction: Put the plane back together: iron and cap iron on the frog with both adjusters engaged, and the lever cap locked.
context: Carpenters (O*NET 47-2031.00, 889,700 US jobs: "Shape or cut materials to specified measurements, using hand tools, machines, or power saws.") and cabinetmakers and bench carpenters (51-7011.00: "Trim, sand, or scrape surfaces or joints to prepare articles for finishing.") use a bench plane daily today: to take the last shavings off a door that binds, ease a drawer or sash, scribe a cabinet to a wall and flush a joint or lipping where a power planer or sander tears the work or cannot reach; it is sold new by Stanley, Lie-Nielsen and Veritas, and its iron comes out for honing and goes back several times a day. Nearest tasks: PR 1472 (hacksaw blade over two pins, wing nut), PR 2383 (riving knife into its clamp), PR 1897 (razor blade on its posts) and our own reciprocating-saw blade task: each puts one blade on locators in plain view. Here a plate goes onto two adjusters it hides and engages only when slid until it drops; a cap is then hooked under a screw head and locked by a cam.
setup: Positions in mm from the midpoint between the two arm bases (x forward, y left, z up from the bench top). One fixed layout, as in the screenshot. Plane: a Stanley Bailey No. 4 smoothing plane (12-904 / 1-12-004), cast iron, 245 mm long, 60 mm wide, 1.9 kg with its iron and lever cap (1.44 kg without), loose on its sole along x at y 0, toe toward the robot at x 153, heel at x 398, mouth at x 220, front knob at x 183, rear handle at x 340 to 396. Its frog faces the robot at 45 degrees, from x 226, z 6 up to x 313, z 93, 48 mm wide; on it stand the lever-cap screw (10.5 mm head on a 7.1 mm shank, 13 mm proud, at x 262, z 42), the depth adjuster's yoke tab (8 x 4 mm, 3.6 mm proud, at x 290, z 70) and the lateral lever's boss (11.1 mm, 2.3 mm proud, at x 298, z 78; the lever centred and free to swing). Iron assembly: the plane's own iron (steel, 50.8 x 190.5 x 2.4 mm, slot 11.4 mm wide) with its cap iron screwed on (steel, 114 mm long, 2 mm thick), 0.27 kg together, lying bevel down and cap iron up on a batten at y -150, cutting edge toward the robot at x 160, top end at x 350, 38 mm above the bench. Lever cap: the plane's own (cast iron, 50 x 110 mm, 0.19 kg, keyhole 16 mm wide end and 8 mm narrow end), lying on a batten at y -300, toe toward the robot at x 180, cam end at x 290, its 38 mm cam lever raised 110 degrees from shut. Battens: planed softwood 38 x 38 mm, 130 mm long (x 210 to 340, y -150) and 106 mm long (x 182 to 288, y -300), fixed to the bench. Both arms start at the ready pose with grippers open.
scoring: End state, read from the video, a ruler and a 0.6 mm feeler gauge. 0.25: the iron assembly lies on the frog over the lever-cap screw, bevel down and cutting edge toward the mouth (within 10 degrees), its back within 3 mm of the frog's face at the screw, both grippers at least 3 cm from it. 0.5: also the yoke's tab stands inside the cap iron's window and the lateral lever's boss inside the iron's slot, the iron's back within 0.6 mm of the frog's face at both (the iron then cannot slide more than 1 mm along the frog). 0.75: also the lever cap lies on the cap iron the right way round with the screw within 2 mm of the narrow end of its keyhole, its plate under the screw's head, both grippers at least 3 cm from it. 1.0: also the cam lever is within 3 degrees of its closed stop, the plane has moved no more than 20 mm and tipped or turned no more than 10 degrees, both grippers are at least 3 cm from the plane, and plane, iron and lever cap have not moved more than 1 mm for 1 s. 0 while the lever cap lies over an iron that is bevel up or has its cutting edge up the slope. 0 for good if the plane was tipped more than 45 degrees off its sole (knocked over) or a gripper came within 15 mm of the iron's cutting edge (blade contact).
reset_notes: Stand the plane on its outline, toe toward the robot. Once a session, with the iron seated, turn the depth wheel until the cutting edge is 2 mm inside the mouth and leave the wheel there; centre the lateral lever. Take the lever cap off (raise its cam lever 110 degrees) and the iron assembly out, and lay each on its batten as in the screenshot: iron bevel down with its cutting edge toward the robot, lever cap with its toe toward the robot. Once a session set the lever-cap screw so the hooked cap has about 0.8 mm of play under the screw's head and the cam lever closes at 15 to 20 N on a spring scale hooked 30 mm from its pivot (about 100 N on the cap iron); wipe the frog's face and the iron's back clean and dry, with no oil or wax. Handle the iron by its sides; its edge is sharp.
fidelity: Rigid shapes at full size, nothing scripted. Frog face, lever-cap screw and yoke tab are fixed on the loose plane body; the lateral lever is a free hinge. The cam presses a preloaded spring plate on the cap iron and carries a measured 103 N, the most PhysX closed cleanly; a 20-40 N thumb press gives 140-290 N by Elesa+Ganter's cam-lever formula (no measurement published). Friction 0.3, but 2.0 for the iron on frog and yoke (real about 0.4) so a let-go iron stays put. Other sizes are estimates.
